title: Hypoxia
subject: Medicine
summary: Hypoxia is inadequate oxygen delivery to tissues, causing cellular dysfunction. Recognise causes, severity, and bedside clues to guide urgent management, especially where diagnostics are limited.

sections.p: Hypoxia occurs when arterial oxygen content (CaO2) falls below that needed for cellular metabolism. Clinically it is identified by low SpO2, PaO2 < 60 mmHg, or cyanosis with normal cardiac output.
b: SpO2 < 90% on room air suggests hypoxemia
PaO2 < 60 mmHg confirms hypoxia on ABG
Cyanosis appears when venous O2 saturation < 85%

sections.p: Severity is staged by PaO2 and clinical impact, guiding urgency of intervention.
b: Mild: PaO2 55‑60 mmHg, mild dyspnoea, no organ dysfunction
Moderate: PaO2 45‑55 mmHg, tachypnoea, early organ stress
Severe: PaO2 < 45 mmHg, altered mental status, shock risk

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most common precipitants are grouped by the site of impairment.
b: Airway obstruction – severe asthma, foreign body, epiglottitis
Alveolar gas exchange – pneumonia (including TB), malaria‑related ARDS, pulmonary embolism, COVID‑19
Circulatory – severe anaemia (malaria, sickle cell), septic shock, severe heart failure (rheumatic heart disease)
Environmental – high altitude, indoor smoke exposure

sections.p: Patients present with dyspnoea, tachypnoea, tachycardia, and variable mental status. Look for clues to the underlying cause.
b: Pleuritic chest pain → pulmonary embolism or pneumonia
Productive cough with night sweats → TB
History of recent malaria treatment → ARDS
Severe anaemia signs (pallor, fatigue) → reduced CaO2

t.b: Is there hypoxaemia? – SpO2 < 90% confirms need for supplemental O2
What is the PaO2 and acid‑base status? – PaO2 < 60 mmHg defines hypoxia; look for respiratory alkalosis
What structural lung disease is present? – Consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax; if unavailable, rely on clinical pattern
Is anaemia contributing? – Hb < 8 g/dL in adults suggests low oxygen‑carrying capacity

t.a: D‑dimer (if PE suspected and test available)
t.b: Is thrombo‑embolism likely? – Elevated D‑dimer supports PE; if unavailable, use Wells score and clinical judgement
Does it show pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or right‑heart strain? – Guides immediate management when X‑ray not possible

sections.p: Uncorrected hypoxia rapidly leads to organ failure.
b: Altered consciousness or seizures
Cardiac arrhythmias or hypotension
Acute respiratory failure requiring ventilation
Multi‑organ dysfunction (renal, hepatic)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then provide oxygen and monitor response.
b: Give supplemental O2 via nasal cannula or mask to keep SpO2 ≥ 94% (≥ 90% in COPD).
If airway obstruction – position, suction, bronchodilators, or emergency intubation.
For pneumonia/TB – start empiric antibiotics or anti‑TB therapy promptly.
Severe anaemia – arrange blood transfusion or iron/folate therapy.
Pulmonary embolism – if confirmed or high suspicion, give anticoagulation (e.g., low‑molecular‑weight heparin) unless contraindicated.

sections.p: Re‑assess oxygenation after each intervention and arrange definitive care.
b: Repeat SpO2/ABG after 30 min of therapy.
Educate on malaria prophylaxis, TB screening, and smoking cessation.
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza to reduce infectious triggers.

sections.p: Hypoxia is distinct from hypoxaemia (low arterial O2) and anaemia (low Hb). All can cause low tissue O2 but need different treatments.
b: Hypoxaemia → treat ventilation/perfusion problems.
Anaemia → treat with transfusion or iron, not oxygen alone.
Normal PaCO2 in early respiratory failure – may hide rising PaO2 deficit.
Cyanosis may be absent in dark‑skinned patients; rely on SpO2.
Pulse oximetry can over‑read in severe carbon monoxide poisoning.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with tachycardia and hypotension

faq.q: Why can a patient with normal chest X‑ray still be hypoxic?
faq.a: Early pulmonary embolism or diffusion impairment may not show radiographic changes; rely on clinical signs and ABG.

faq.q: Can anaemia cause hypoxia even with normal PaO2?
faq.a: Yes, low haemoglobin reduces oxygen‑carrying capacity, so tissues can be hypoxic despite normal arterial oxygen tension.

faq.q: When is high‑flow nasal cannula preferred over a simple mask?
faq.a: When the patient needs higher FiO2 and some positive airway pressure, but mechanical ventilation is not yet indicated.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer with sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and SpO2 88% – what is your next immediate step? — Give supplemental O2, assess for PE using Wells score, and arrange urgent imaging if feasible.
Explain why a patient with severe malaria may develop hypoxia despite clear lungs. — Parasite‑induced sequestration causes pulmonary capillary leak and ARDS, impairing gas exchange.
How does anaemia contribute to tissue hypoxia and how would you manage it in a low‑resource setting? — Low Hb reduces CaO2; treat with transfusion if Hb < 6 g/dL or iron/folate for chronic anaemia.

Distinguish hypoxaemia from hypoxia in a patient with COPD presenting with dyspnoea. — Hypoxaemia is low PaO2; hypoxia is tissue O2 deficit, which in COPD may be worsened by ventilation‑perfusion mismatch and low Hb.
What bedside sign suggests a pneumothorax causing hypoxia and how would you confirm it without X‑ray? — Decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance; confirm with POCUS showing absent lung sliding.

Why is routine use of high‑dose steroids discouraged in hypoxic patients with infection? — Steroids can suppress immunity and worsen infection; only indicated in specific conditions like severe COVID‑19 or adrenal insufficiency.
A patient on high‑flow O2 still has PaO2 50 mmHg – what does this indicate and what is the next step? — Refractory hypoxemia; consider intubation and mechanical ventilation.
List three red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral for a hypoxic patient. — Altered mental status, hemodynamic instability, and rapidly falling SpO2 despite oxygen.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic physical exam quickly differentiate hypoxia from other causes of dyspnoea and reveal the anatomic level of impairment.
b: Onset: sudden vs gradual; minutes suggest airway obstruction, embolism, pneumothorax; days suggest infection or anaemia.
Precipitating events: recent malaria treatment, trauma, asthma attack, high‑altitude exposure, surgery.
Associated symptoms: pleuritic chest pain, cough with sputum, fever, night sweats, wheeze, chest tightness, haemoptysis.
Risk factors: HIV, TB, sickle cell disease, chronic heart disease, pregnancy, malnutrition, smoking, indoor biomass smoke.
Systemic signs: fever, chills, recent blood loss, jaundice, pallor, edema, recent transfusion.
Functional impact: confusion, agitation, reduced exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, nocturnal dyspnoea.

t.b: Looks for cyanosis, use of accessory muscles, chest wall asymmetry, and altered mental status; cyanosis appears when arterial O2 saturation falls below ~80‑85% or deoxy‑Hb >5 g/dL.
Assess tactile fremitus (increased in consolidation, decreased in pleural effusion or pneumothorax) and chest expansion symmetry.
Hyper‑resonance suggests pneumothorax; dullness suggests consolidation, effusion, or severe atelectasis. Cannot differentiate fluid from solid without further testing.

Crackles indicate alveolar filling (pneumonia, ARDS); wheeze points to airway obstruction; absent breath sounds locally suggest pneumothorax or massive effusion. Auscultation cannot quantify gas exchange.
Provides SpO2; <90 % on room air signals hypoxaemia but does not distinguish cause or severity of tissue hypoxia.
Prolonged refill (>2 s) or cool extremities suggest circulatory compromise contributing to hypoxia; cannot diagnose pulmonary pathology.
Detects pneumothorax (lung sliding absent), pleural effusion, and B‑lines for interstitial edema; not definitive for pulmonary embolism without Doppler.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; interpret results with locally relevant cut‑offs and have fallback plans when a test is unavailable.
b: Arterial blood gas (ABG): confirms hypoxaemia (PaO2 < 60 mmHg) and assesses acid‑base status; PaO2/FiO2 < 300 suggests ARDS when bilateral infiltrates are present.
Complete blood count: haemoglobin <7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL in cardiac disease) indicates anaemia‑related hypoxia; leukocytosis supports infection.
Chest radiograph: looks for infiltrates, consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and bedside ultrasound.
Serum lactate: >2 mmol/L signals cellular stress and possible tissue hypoperfusion; repeat to trend response to therapy.
D‑dimer (if PE suspected): elevated value raises suspicion; definitive diagnosis requires imaging, often unavailable—use clinical probability scores.
ECG: right‑sided strain patterns suggest massive PE; ST changes may indicate myocardial ischemia contributing to hypoxia.
Point‑of‑care ultrasound: lung sliding, B‑lines, pleural effusion; absence of sliding confirms pneumothorax; if ultrasound not available, use percussion and auscultation.

t.b: Answers: Is the patient truly hypoxaemic? PaO2 < 60 mmHg confirms hypoxaemia; PaO2 < 40 mmHg defines severe hypoxia. If ABG unavailable, use SpO2 < 90 % as a surrogate.
Answers: Is there hypoventilation or respiratory failure? PaCO2 > 45 mmHg indicates hypoventilation; PaCO2 < 35 mmHg suggests hyperventilation.
Answers: Is hypoxaemia due to V/Q mismatch or diffusion defect? A‑a gradient > (Age/4 + 4) mmHg is abnormal; high gradient points to alveolar disease.
Answers: Is there pneumonia, ARDS, or effusion? Bilateral diffuse infiltrates with PaO2/FiO2 < 300 meet ARDS criteria. If X‑ray unavailable, rely on clinical picture and ultrasound.
Answers: Is a pneumothorax present? Absence of sliding with a lung point confirms pneumothorax. Cannot assess gas exchange.
Answers: Is anaemia contributing? Hb < 7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL in cardiac disease) suggests severe anaemia; transfuse if symptomatic.
Answers: Is there cellular hypoxia from hypoperfusion? Lactate > 2 mmol/L indicates stress; trend down with resuscitation.
Answers: Is pulmonary embolism likely? Elevated D‑dimer raises suspicion; if imaging unavailable, treat empirically if high clinical probability.

sections.p: Classification integrates arterial oxygen tension, clinical impact, and underlying mechanism to guide urgency of intervention.
b: Mild hypoxia: PaO2 60‑79 mmHg or SpO2 90‑94 %; mild dyspnoea, no organ dysfunction; monitor, low‑flow O₂ if needed.
Severe hypoxia: PaO2 < 40 mmHg or SpO2 < 85 %; altered mental status, hypotension, shock risk; high‑flow O₂ or non‑rebreather, consider CPAP/BiPAP, early escalation.
Critical hypoxia: PaO2 < 30 mmHg despite maximal O₂; impending respiratory arrest; requires invasive ventilation and intensive monitoring.
Staging by mechanism: airway obstruction, alveolar gas‑exchange disorder, circulatory limitation, environmental exposure; each stage directs specific therapy.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic hypoxia; distinguishing features are highlighted to avoid misdiagnosis.

t.b: Points: CO2 retention, drowsiness, normal PaO2 early; ABG shows PaCO2 > 45 mmHg. Separate by measuring PaCO2; treat with ventilation rather than O₂ alone.
Points: Low HCO3‑, low PaCO2, normal PaO2; patient may appear dyspnoeic but oxygenation is adequate. ABG differentiates; treat underlying metabolic cause.
Points: Low Hb, normal PaO2, cyanosis absent; pulse oximetry may be normal. CBC confirms; management focuses on transfusion, not oxygen.
Points: Cherry‑red skin, normal PaO2, low SpO2 reading due to sensor error; co‑oximetry needed. Give 100 % O₂; avoid mistaking for simple hypoxia.
Points: Chocolate‑brown blood, SpO2 ~85 % unresponsive to O₂, normal PaO2. Co‑oximetry required; treat with methylene blue, not high‑flow O₂ alone.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures rapid reversal of hypoxia while addressing the underlying cause, using resources available in low‑resource settings.
b: 1. Immediate airway assessment – clear obstruction, chin‑lift, jaw‑thrust, suction if needed.
3. If SpO₂ remains <90% despite simple mask, apply non‑rebreather mask (10–15 L/min) while preparing for possible advanced airway.
4. Identify and treat the primary cause – e.g., bronchodilators for severe asthma, antimalarials for malaria‑related ARDS, anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism, antibiotics for pneumonia/TB.
5. Initiate fluid resuscitation only if hypovolemia is present; avoid fluid overload in ARDS or cardiac failure.
6. Consider blood transfusion when Hb <7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL with cardiac disease) after ruling out active bleeding.
7. Monitor: continuous SpO₂, respiratory rate, mental status, blood pressure, urine output; repeat ABG if available.
8. Escalate to high‑flow oxygen, CPAP/BiPAP, or intubation when respiratory fatigue, PaO₂ <40 mmHg, or severe acidosis develops; refer to higher‑level facility if ventilation not possible locally.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Common pharmacologic interventions have predictable adverse effects; awareness allows prompt mitigation.
b: β2‑agonists (e.g., salbutamol) may cause tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia – check pulse, give potassium‑rich foods if needed.
Systemic corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation but raise blood glucose and risk infection – monitor glucose, avoid high‑dose steroids in untreated infection.
Heparin for pulmonary embolism can cause bleeding – check platelet count, watch for haematuria or melena; reverse with protamine if major bleed.
Antimalarials (artesunate) may cause transient anaemia – monitor haemoglobin, avoid unnecessary transfusion.
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics can cause diarrhoea and C. difficile – use narrowest effective agent once cultures return.
Tranexamic acid for massive haemorrhage can increase thrombosis risk – use only when bleeding is uncontrolled.

sections.p: Recognize early signs of organ compromise to trigger higher‑level care.
b: Progressive mental status change (confusion → agitation → coma) indicates cerebral hypoxia – prepare for airway protection and ventilation.
New onset arrhythmia or hypotension suggests cardiac hypoxia – start inotropic support, consider ICU transfer.
Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h) or rising creatinine points to renal hypoperfusion – adjust fluids, avoid nephrotoxins.
Lactate >2 mmol/L with worsening acidosis signals systemic hypoperfusion – intensify oxygen delivery and consider vasopressors.
Persistent PaO₂ <40 mmHg despite maximal non‑invasive oxygen – intubate and ventilate or refer for mechanical ventilation.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities modify presentation, investigations, and therapy of hypoxia.
b: HIV/TB: may present with atypical pneumonia; sputum GeneXpert preferred, but if unavailable use chest X‑ray patterns and clinical response.
Malnutrition lowers albumin, altering drug binding and increasing risk of hypovolaemia; give micronutrient‑rich feeds early.
Pregnancy: maternal PaO₂ <70 mmHg threatens fetus – maintain SpO₂ ≥95%; avoid teratogenic drugs, use low‑dose steroids only when indicated.
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia worsens infection; monitor glucose, adjust insulin when steroids are given.
Alcohol use: predisposes to aspiration and ARDS – consider early antibiotics and protective ventilation.
Renal failure: limits diuretic use, alters fluid balance – use cautious crystalloid boluses, monitor electrolytes.
Liver disease: reduces synthesis of clotting factors; avoid NSAIDs that increase bleeding risk.
Extreme ages: infants have higher metabolic O₂ demand; elderly have blunted ventilatory response – set higher SpO₂ targets (≥94%).

sections.p: Tailor assessment and treatment to the physiological differences of each population.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate oxygen flow (e.g., 1–2 L/min nasal cannula); consider bronchiolitis, congenital heart disease; avoid high‑pressure masks.
Pregnancy: position mother left lateral to improve uteroplacental flow; give supplemental O₂ via face mask; avoid drugs that cross placenta without clear benefit.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections (PJP, TB); use trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for PJP prophylaxis; monitor CD4 count.
Low‑resource settings: rely on clinical scoring (e.g., respiratory rate, mental status) when ABG unavailable; use portable pulse oximetry; prioritize oxygen concentrators over cylinders.

facts: Mild hypoxia: PaO2 60‑79 mmHg or SpO2 90‑94%
Severe hypoxia: PaO2 <40 mmHg or SpO2 <85%
Cyanosis appears when venous O2 saturation falls below ~67% (or deoxy‑Hb >5 g/dL)
Serum lactate >2 mmol/L signals cellular stress and possible hypoperfusion
Hemoglobin <7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL in cardiac disease) warrants transfusion for anemia‑related hypoxia
PaO2/FiO2 <300 defines ARDS when bilateral infiltrates and no cardiac failure are present
In pregnancy, maternal PaO2 <70 mmHg is considered hypoxemic for the fetus
Delivery after shoulder dystocia should be completed within 5 minutes of first maneuver
HIF‑1α stabilization drives VEGF expression in tumor hypoxia

mnemonics.t: Hypoxia, Acidosis, Respiratory distress, Dyspnoea – key bedside clues to severe hypoxia
Circulation, Airway, Breathing, Confidence – order of immediate management in low‑resource settings

vivas.q: Define hypoxia and differentiate it from hypoxaemia.
vivas.a: Hypoxia is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery; hypoxaemia is low arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) or saturation. Hypoxaemia may cause hypoxia but other factors (anaemia, low cardiac output) also do.

vivas.q: What bedside sign suggests a pneumothorax causing hypoxia and how would you confirm it without X‑ray?
vivas.a: Absent unilateral breath sounds with hyper‑resonance on percussion; confirm with bedside ultrasound showing absent lung sliding (lung point).

vivas.q: Why is high‑dose steroids avoided in infection‑related hypoxia?
vivas.a: High‑dose steroids suppress immunity, worsen bacterial clearance and increase risk of secondary infection; they are only indicated in specific conditions (e.g., severe CAP with refractory shock).

vivas.q: A patient on high‑flow O2 still has PaO2 50 mmHg. What does this indicate and what is the next step?
vivas.a: Refractory hypoxemia suggests shunt physiology (e.g., pneumonia, ARDS); next step is to consider non‑invasive ventilation or early intubation with PEEP.

vivas.q: List three red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral for a hypoxic patient.
vivas.a: Altered mental status, persistent SpO2 <85% despite supplemental O2, and hemodynamic instability (hypotension or shock).

vivas.q: How does severe anaemia cause tissue hypoxia and what is the low‑resource management?
vivas.a: Anaemia reduces CaO2 despite normal PaO2; management includes rapid transfusion if Hb <7 g/dL, treat underlying cause, and give oxygen to optimise delivery.

vivas.q: Explain the pathophysiology of malaria‑related ARDS despite clear lungs on exam.
vivas.a: Sequestration of parasitized RBCs and inflammatory cytokines increase pulmonary capillary permeability, causing non‑cardiogenic edema and hypoxia even without overt crackles.

vivas.q: Distinguish hypoxaemia from hypoxia in a COPD patient presenting with dyspnoea.
vivas.a: COPD patients may have normal PaO2 but low PaO2/FiO2 due to V/Q mismatch; tissue hypoxia can occur from chronic CO2 retention and reduced O2 delivery despite acceptable arterial values.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a serum lactate >2 mmol/L in a hypoxic patient?
vivas.a: It indicates cellular stress and possible tissue hypoperfusion; rising lactate warrants aggressive resuscitation and monitoring.

vivas.q: Why is a PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300 used for ARDS diagnosis and not for ‘acute lung injury’?
vivas.a: The term acute lung injury has been replaced; a ratio <300 with bilateral infiltrates and no cardiac cause defines ARDS per Berlin criteria.

vivas.q: What are the four major pulmonary effects of meconium aspiration that lead to hypoxia?
vivas.a: Airway obstruction, surfactant inactivation, chemical pneumonitis causing edema, and atelectasis from alveolar collapse.

vivas.q: In a patient with sickle cell acute chest syndrome, what is the key mechanism of hypoxia?
vivas.a: In‑situ pulmonary vaso‑occlusion by sickled cells plus infection‑induced inflammation causing ventilation‑perfusion mismatch.

vivas.q: How would you assess for cyanosis at the bedside and what threshold does it reflect?
vivas.a: Inspect lips, nail beds, and mucous membranes; cyanosis appears when deoxy‑Hb >5 g/dL, roughly arterial saturation <80‑85% or venous saturation <67%.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line oxygen delivery device for a patient with SpO2 88% on room air in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Nasal cannula at 2‑4 L/min; if SpO2 remains <90%, progress to simple face mask (6‑10 L/min) then non‑rebreather.

vivas.q: How long does irreversible neuronal injury occur after global cerebral hypoxia?
vivas.a: Approximately 4‑6 minutes of complete oxygen deprivation leads to irreversible neuronal death.

vivas.q: Which organ systems receive priority blood flow during systemic hypoxia and catecholamine surge?
vivas.a: Brain, heart, and adrenal cortex are preferentially perfused; peripheral vasoconstriction shunts blood away from skin and gut.

vivas.q: What proportion of infected patients with COVID‑19 progress to stage 3 disease with pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxia?
vivas.a: Roughly 15‑20% develop severe disease with infiltrates and hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen.

vivas.q: In a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism and hypoxia, what bedside test can support the diagnosis when imaging is unavailable?
vivas.a: Echocardiographic right‑ventricular dilation or McConnell’s sign suggests acute PE; combined with tachycardia and hypoxia, it guides empiric anticoagulation.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old male with severe asthma presents with SpO2 84% despite 6 L/min O2 via simple mask. Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Intubate and provide mechanical ventilation with PEEP
mcqs.e: Severe asthma with refractory hypoxia requires airway protection and PEEP to overcome dynamic hyperinflation.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks has PaO2 68 mmHg on room air. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Irrelevant; focus on fetal monitoring only
mcqs.e: Maternal PaO2 <70 mmHg is hypoxaemic and warrants oxygen therapy to protect the fetus.

mcqs.q: Which transcription factor is stabilized in tumor hypoxia and drives VEGF expression?
mcqs.e: HIF‑1α is the key hypoxia‑inducible factor that up‑regulates VEGF.

mcqs.q: A child with meconium aspiration shows coarse crackles, hyperinflated chest X‑ray, and SpO2 82% on room air. Which pulmonary effect is NOT typical?
mcqs.e: Bronchial hyperreactivity is not a primary effect of meconium aspiration.

mcqs.q: In severe malaria, a patient develops hypoxia with clear lungs. Which mechanism explains this?
mcqs.e: Parasite‑induced sequestration leads to non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxia.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old with sickle cell disease presents with chest pain, fever, and SpO2 86% after a vaso‑occlusive crisis. What is the primary pathophysiology of his acute chest syndrome?
mcqs.e: Acute chest syndrome results from pulmonary vaso‑occlusion plus infection, causing V/Q mismatch.

mcqs.q: Which lactate level most strongly suggests tissue hypoperfusion in a hypoxic patient?
mcqs.e: Lactate >2 mmol/L is a marker of cellular stress and possible hypoperfusion.

mcqs.q: A patient with suspected ARDS has PaO2 55 mmHg on FiO2 0.6. What is the PaO2/FiO2 ratio and does it meet ARDS criteria?
mcqs.e: PaO2/FiO2 = 55/0.6 ≈ 92, which is <300 and meets ARDS definition if other criteria are present.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 88% on room air, and no wheeze. No fever. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Chest exam: decreased breath sounds left lower zone, hyper‑resonance.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What bedside investigation confirms it without radiography?
qs.a: Point‑of‑care lung ultrasound showing absent lung sliding and a lung point.

qs.q: Initial management in a low‑resource setting?
qs.a: Apply a large‑bore needle thoracostomy (e.g., 14‑G) followed by chest tube insertion if available; give supplemental O2.

cases.v: A 6‑year‑old child with a history of meconium‑stained amniotic fluid at birth now presents with rapid breathing, grunting, SpO2 84% on room air, and diffuse crackles. Chest X‑ray (if available) shows hyperinflated lungs with patchy infiltrates.

qs.q: List the four pulmonary mechanisms by which meconium aspiration causes hypoxia.
qs.a: Airway obstruction, surfactant inactivation, chemical pneumonitis with edema, and atelectasis from alveolar collapse.

qs.q: What is the first‑line oxygen delivery method?
qs.a: Nasal cannula 2‑4 L/min; if inadequate, progress to simple face mask.

qs.q: If the child remains hypoxic despite maximal O2, what is the next step?
qs.a: Consider CPAP or bubble CPAP to recruit alveoli and improve ventilation‑perfusion matching.

mistakes: Using PaO2 55‑60 mmHg as the definition of mild hypoxia – the correct range is 60‑79 mmHg.
Stating cyanosis appears at venous O2 saturation <85% – the true threshold is ~67% or deoxy‑Hb >5 g/dL.
Assuming a PaO2/FiO2 <300 only indicates ‘acute lung injury’; it defines ARDS when other criteria are met.
Transfusing blood for anaemia at Hb <8 g/dL in all patients – the threshold is <7 g/dL (or <8 g/dL only in high‑risk cardiac disease).
Recommending non‑rebreather mask solely because SpO2 <90% – escalation should follow a stepwise O2 delivery ladder.
Claiming high‑dose steroids are universally contraindicated in infection‑related hypoxia – they are indicated in specific conditions such as severe CAP or PCP.
Confusing fetal hypoxia threshold with maternal PaO2 <70 mmHg – this is the correct maternal threshold, not a fetal value.
Suggesting delivery after shoulder dystocia must be within 10 minutes – the evidence supports completion within 5 minutes.
